title: Cause and consequence
job: Why things happen and what follows, across a paragraph
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: quod AND quia BOTH MEAN 'BECAUSE' AND THIS COURSE WRITES ONLY quia. L1-M9 took quod for the causal reading, and L3-M2 gave up two shapes of the relative pronoun — the neuter and the feminine object — to keep that key carrying one true note. A paragraph of causes is exactly where an author reaches for variety, so the discipline is stated here again: quia is the whole of 'because' in en-la, and quod is L1-M9's and nothing else's.

ideō POINTS FORWARD AND itaque POINTS BACK, AND BOTH COME FIRST IN THEIR CLAUSE. ideō … quia is 'for this reason … because' — a frame English does not have, because 'for this reason' followed by 'because' sounds redundant in English and is standard in Latin: ideō announces that a cause is coming and quia delivers it. itaque draws the consequence after the fact instead. So a chain can be ordered either way and the connective says which end is being explained — and a sentence needs exactly ONE of quia, ideō or itaque, never two.

THE ABLATIVE OF CAUSE IS THE SIXTH JOB THAT CASE HAS DONE, and again with no preposition: timōre nōn vēnī, 'I did not come out of fear'. After opus est (L1-M3), in and cum (L1-M7), means (L2-M4), time (L2-M6) and comparison (L2-M9), this is the sixth, and every one of the six works by the ending alone. propter plus the OBJECT shape is the same idea with a preposition — the pair L2-M4 set up for means, with in raedā against raedā, and the choice is style rather than meaning.

THE COURSE NOW HAS SEVEN CONNECTIVES THAT MUST COME FIRST AND SIX THAT MUST COME SECOND, and the list is worth more than the principle. First: itaque, ergō, ideō, prīmum, deinde, tum, postrēmō. Second: autem, enim, igitur, quoque, vērō, tamen. And quia, quod, dum, postquam and antequam join two clauses from the front. Thirteen words in three groups, and nothing about a word's meaning tells you which group it is in.

'TO BE' JOINS TWO SUBJECTS AND NEVER TAKES AN OBJECT: causa timor fuit, 'the reason was fear' — two nominatives in one clause. The course has used this since L1-M1 without naming it, and a module about causes is where it becomes visible, because naming a cause is exactly the sentence that needs two subjects.

A CAUSE CAN COME FIRST OR LAST AND quia GOES WITH IT EITHER WAY. Quia timōre nōn vēnī, mē pudet puts the cause first; mē pudet, quia timōre nōn vēnī puts it last. Both are correct and the second is commoner. What is never correct is quia in front and itaque behind — two connectives for one relation, which is the 'because … therefore' error English speakers make in English too and notice far less.

THE JOB IS A PARAGRAPH OF CAUSES, NOT A SENTENCE OF THEM. The module's later sentences run three and four clauses, and the machinery is entirely the ladder's: a case for the cause, a connective for the order, L3-M2's possum for what could not be done, L3-M6's impersonals for how it felt. Only ideō, propter, timor and causa are new, which is what leaves room for the length.

sentences.cue: I did not come, because I was ill.

words.note: 'Not', in front of what it denies. L1-M3's word.
'I came' — the perfect of veniō, one bar from venit.
'Because'. L1-M9's word, and the ONLY 'because' this course writes: quod means it too and its key already carries L1-M9's note.
'Ill' — aeger, aegra, aegrum, and the e drops as soon as an ending is added. L3-M7's word.
'I was' — the perfect of sum, and the only past of it this course writes. The tense for a state that went ON is still to come.

sentences.trap: quia and not quod. Both mean 'because' in Latin and this course writes only quia, because L1-M9 took quod for that reading and L3-M2 had to name the neuter relative as unwritable as a result. A paragraph of causes is where an author reaches for variety and would spend a key that has one true note.

'Not', in front of what it denies.

sentences.trap: itaque points BACK and ideō points FORWARD, and both come first in their clause. So a cause can be announced before it (ideō … quia) or drawn after it (… itaque …), and the two frames are mirror images — which is worth knowing because English uses 'so' for the second and has nothing for the first.

sentences.trap: A cause, an event and a consequence in six words, and the sentence is a small paragraph. That is the module's job: not a sentence of causes but a chain of them, and the machinery for it — a case, a connective and two perfects — has been in the learner's hands since L2.

words.note: 'Because'. L1-M9's word, and the ONLY 'because' this course writes: quod means it too and its key already carries L1-M9's note.
'Out of fear' — the bare ablative doing cause.
'Not', in front of what it denies.
'I came' — the perfect of veniō.
'Me' — the ACCUSATIVE, because pudet wants it. L3-M6's row, and the family libet and placet do not belong to.
'It shames' — impersonal, and it takes the accusative of the person. L3-M6's verb.

sentences.trap: quia can open a sentence as well as follow one, which English does too — and when it opens, the consequence comes after it with no connective at all. So a causal sentence in Latin needs exactly one of quia, ideō or itaque and never two.
sentences.sound: QUI-a ti-MŌ-re nōn VĒ-nī, MĒ PU-det. Eleven syllables, and the shame is the shortest part of it.

mistake.display: Quia timōre nōn vēnī, itaque mē pudet.
mistake.why: two connectives for one relation. quia already says the first clause is the cause, so itaque says it a second time — and this is the error English speakers make with 'because … therefore', which is equally wrong there and much less noticeable.

sentences.usage: Said when the cause matters more than the result.

'For this reason', and it points FORWARD to the cause. Its usual partner is quia: ideō … quia, 'for this reason … because', which is a frame English does not have.
